section.title: Activity (15 minutes)
section.para: In this activity, students use the structure they saw earlier to rewrite squared expressions of the form \((kx+m)^2\), where \(k\) is not 1, into standard form. Through repeated reasoning, students see how the coefficient \(k\) is related to the values of \(a\) and \(b\) when the expression is expanded into \(ax^2+bx+c\), and how the \(m\) is related to \(c\).
As students work, monitor for the following strategies for rewriting the expressions in the first question (from factored form to standard form):

list.item: Drawing rectangular diagrams.
Applying the distributive property, writing out all the expanded terms, and combining like terms.
Generalizing that when expanding an expression such as \((4x+1)^2\):
The coefficient 4 in \(4x+1\) gets squared, so \(a\) in \(ax^2+bx+c\) is \(4^2\).
The coefficient 4 in \(4x+1\) gets multiplied by the constant term 1 twice, so \(b\) is \(2(4)(1)\).
The constant term 1 in \(4x+1\) is squared, so \(c\) is \(1^2\).

section.para: Identify students using each strategy and invite them to share during the class discussion.
section.title: Launch
section.para: Explain to students that they will now practice squaring expressions such as \(4x+1\) and \(\frac{1}{2}x+7\), where the coefficient of the linear term is not 1, and writing them in standard form.
Consider arranging students in groups of two and asking them to think individually about each question before conferring with their partner.

para.title: MLR 7 Compare and Connect: Representing, Conversing

div.para: As students share their strategies for the first question, call students' attention to the different approaches to rewriting the expressions in standard form. Take a close look at the last two parts of the first problem and how the value of \(k\) is represented in the expression 9x²+ 2 (3)(n)x + n² . Wherever possible, amplify student words and actions that describe the connections between a specific feature of one mathematical representation and a specific feature of another representation.
Design Principle(s): Maximize meta-awareness; Cultivate conversation
View the instructional video and follow along with the materials to assist you with learning this routine.
Distribute graphic organizers to the students to assist them with participating in this routine.

para.title: Action and Expression: Develop Expression and Communication

div.para: To help get students started, display sentence frames that elicit observations about the connection between squared and standard form for each expression. For example, “I notice that . . . .” and “It looks like . . . .” After students have discussed these initial observations, display frames that encourage students, in their partner groups, to create generalizations from their observations that they can share with the whole class. For example, “_____ will always _____ because . . . .” and “Is it always true that . . . ?”

section.title: Activity Synthesis
section.para: Select previously identified students to share their responses and strategies for the first question, starting with students who used diagrams and ending with students who generalized the pattern in the rewriting process. As students explain, display or record their reasoning for all to see.
If not mentioned in students' explanations, highlight the generalization noted in the activity narrative.

Then, discuss how students used their insights from the first question to help them identify perfect squares, or to turn expressions into perfect squares, in the second question. Make sure students see the structure behind the values of \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) when the expression \(ax^2+bx+c\) is a perfect square. This structure will help them complete the square in the next activity.
section.title: 9.4.2: Self Check

para.emphasis: After the activity, students will answer the following question to check their understanding of the concepts explored in the activity.

section.para: QUESTION:
Find the equivalent factored expression for \(4x^2+12x+9\).

section.title: Factoring Perfect Square Trinomials
section.para: To factor perfect square trinomials, follow the formulas:
Let's look at an example of how to factor perfect square trinomials.
Step 1 - Does the trinomial fit the perfect square trinomial pattern, \(a^2+2ab+b^2\)? If so, write the first term as \(a^2\) and last constant as \(b^2\).

list.item:
Is the first term a perfect square? Write it as a square, \(a^2\).
Is \(9x^2\) a perfect square?
Yes — write it as \((3x)^2\).
\(\begin{array}{l}9x^2\;+\;12x\;+\;4 \\ (3x)^2\;\end{array}\)

Is the last term a perfect square? Write it as a square, \(b^2\).
Is 4 a perfect square?
Yes — write it as \((2)^2\).
\(\begin{array}{l}9x^2\;+\;12x\;+\;4 \\ (3x)^2\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;(2)^2\end{array}\)

Check the middle term. Is it \(2ab\)?
Is \(12x\) twice the product of \(3x\) and 2?
Does it match?
Yes, so we have a perfect trinomial.

section.para:
Step 2 - Factor the binomial into: \(a^2+2ab+b^2 = (a+b)^2 \)
\(9x^2+12x+4\)
\(\begin{array}{l}a^2\;\;\;\;\;\;+2\cdot a\cdot b+b^2 \\ \;({\style{color:red}3}{\style{color:red}x})^2\;+2 \cdot {\style{color:red}3}{\style{color:red}x} \cdot {\style{color:purple}2}+{\style{color:purple}2}^2\; \\ \;\;\;\;\;\;\;(a+b)^2\; \\ \;\;\;\;\;({\style{color:red}3}{\style{color:red}x}+{\style{color:green}2})^{\style{color:green}2}\end{array}\)

section.title: Solution
section.para: Here is how to factor a perfect square trinomial:

Step 1 - Write the first term as \(a^2\) and the last constant as \(b^2\).
\(a^2=(3x)^2\), \(b^2=5^2\)

Make sure the middle term is \(2ab\).
\(2ab=2(3x)(5)=30x\)

Step 2 - Factor the binomial into: \(a^2-2ab+b^2=(a-b)^2\).
\((3x-5)^2\)
Step 3 - Check.
